module.name: docs
module.spec:
Overview: This meta-spec establishes the rules every other spec in the docs module follows. Chapter specs, concept specs, and sync specs MUST satisfy these requirements. This spec is the pedagogical authority for the documentation system.
Drift is a sync layer between specs and code. The agent writes both. Drift keeps them aligned. The documentation is task-oriented: each chapter is a real task a developer performs, not an abstract concept. Concepts are introduced in service of tasks, reinforced through reuse in other tasks. See glossary.spec for the formal definition of a spec and glossary.ref for the ref mechanism used throughout.
R1. Learning objectives. Every chapter spec MUST list 3-7 learning objectives. Each objective MUST use a measurable Bloom verb (identify, describe, explain, apply, analyze, evaluate, design, construct, troubleshoot). Objectives MUST NOT use unmeasurable verbs (know, understand, learn, see, grasp, appreciate).
R2. Prerequisites via ref. Every chapter spec MUST declare prerequisites via <ref> tags to concept specs and earlier chapter specs. The prereq graph MUST be acyclic: chapter N may cite chapters 1 through N-1 and any concept spec, but no chapter may cite a later chapter.
R3. Content requirements. Every chapter spec MUST enumerate what the chapter file (docs/NN-*.md) covers to satisfy the learning objectives.
R4. Formative assessment. Every chapter spec MUST require at least one "Try it yourself" exercise. Exercises state a goal and a verification step, not a step-by-step recipe. Each exercise MUST be wrapped in a dedicated marker (named <shortcode>_ex) linked to the same chapter spec. Removing an exercise from a chapter file MUST produce drift on the chapter spec.
R5. Concept specs. Concept specs are atomic and MAY be cited by multiple chapter specs. A concept introduced when first needed in a task chapter is reinforced through reuse in later task chapters (task-driven spiral). Concept specs MUST cite canonical authority (glossary.* for definitions, core.* for algorithmic contracts) via <ref>. Concept specs MUST NOT cite chapter specs. Concepts are foundational; chapters are delivery vehicles.
R6. Sync specs. Topics covered in BOTH docs/ and cli/skill.md MUST have a sync spec. The sync spec enumerates required coverage; markers in both files link to it. Changing the enumeration drifts both markers. Sync specs do NOT catch wording divergence. That requires the periodic spec audit.
R7. Ref ordering. Within a chapter spec prerequisite list, concept specs MUST be cited before chapter specs. This ordering is a convention, not enforced by the scanner.

Overview: A spec is a unit of intended behavior expressed as plain text inside an XML element in a *.drift.xml module file. Specs are compressed intent: the human or agent writes a spec to capture a rule, and the scanner hashes the spec content (with refs stripped) so renaming a referenced spec ID does not invalidate the referrer's hash.
Definition authority: glossary.spec.

Overview: A marker is a pair of comment lines — a range-start and a range-end — wrapping a code region that implements a spec. The shortcode contains no dot. The scanner hashes the lines between the markers, excluding the marker declarations themselves. Markers are the implementation side of the spec-code duality. Markers cannot be cited by specs or other markers.
Definition authority: glossary.marker.

Overview: An edge is a directed relationship between two nodes in the citation graph. Two kinds exist: marker to spec (created by drift link) and spec to spec (auto-parsed from ref tags inside spec content). Both share the same storage and drift semantics. The From endpoint is the citer; the To endpoint is the cited. Drift propagates along the citer chain: when the cited changes, every citer is suspect.
Definition authority: glossary.edge.

Overview: The baseline is the most-recently-reviewed state of the citation graph, persisted in .drift/state.xml with content snapshots in .drift/baselines.bin. A node whose baseline hash matches its current scan hash has not changed since last review. Closures are derived by comparing baseline against scan; drift events are the differences.
Definition authority: glossary.baseline.

Overview: A scan is the current state of specs, markers, and edges discovered by walking workspace files. The scanner reads *.drift.xml for specs and refs, and scans text files for markers. A scan is computed fresh on every drift todo invocation. Comparing baseline against scan produces drift events.
Definition authority: glossary.scan.

Overview: A closure is a per-seed drift set computed when baseline and scan disagree. Each closure contains one seed node plus every spec that transitively cites it (the citer chain). For marker seeds, the linked specs are also included. Closures are ephemeral — not stored in state.xml — and strictly disjoint across seeds. Closure identity is the first 8 hex chars of SHA1(sorted node IDs + sorted undirected edge keys).
Definition authority: glossary.closure (canonical definition), core.provenance_closure (algorithmic contract).

Overview: A drift event is a single difference between baseline and scan. Six types exist: NODE_CHANGED (hash differs), NODE_ADDED (new in scan), NODE_REMOVED (missing from scan), EDGE_ADDED (new spec-spec edge), EDGE_REMOVED (edge gone from scan), EDGE_BROKEN (scan edge whose target does not exist). Each event has a seed: the node where the change originates. Events seed closures.
Definition authority: glossary.seed.

Overview: The citer chain is the set of specs that transitively cite a given spec via ref edges. When a spec changes, drift propagates along the citer chain: every citer is suspect and lands in the closure. This is how changing a foundational spec surfaces drift on every spec that depends on it, transitively to fixpoint.
Definition authority: glossary.citer.

Overview: Friction is drift's design principle that per-closure review cannot be bypassed. There is no bulk reset. A runtime rate-limit blocks the 4th reset within any 30-second window. The friction layer enforces that each closure receives individual attention — the agent cannot blindly dismiss all drift without reviewing each piece.
Definition authority: cli.reset_friction_block.

Overview: The reader learns what spec drift is and why LLM-assisted codebases make it acute. This is a motivation chapter with no commands and no install. The chapter frames the problem drift solves and introduces drift as a sync layer.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/01-why-drift-exists.md, the reader can: - describe the problem of spec drift between intent and code - explain why human review fails to catch drift at agent code volume - identify drift as a sync layer between specs and code
Prerequisites: - spec concept (introduced by analogy) - marker concept (introduced by analogy)
Content requirements: - present a concrete scenario where an LLM agent ships code that violates an implicit project rule - explain why traditional review practices (code review, testing) fail to catch semantic drift at agent output volume - describe drift as a sync layer: specs are compressed intent, code is the expansion, drift keeps them aligned - explain that the agent writes both specs and code; the human steers through specs - link forward to chapter 02 (getting started) as the next step - include a thought exercise (marker: docwhy_ex) asking the reader to identify a recent PR where an agent violated an implicit rule and what spec would have caught it

Overview: The reader installs drift, gives the binary to their agent, and watches the agent bootstrap specs and markers. The chapter frames the agent as the primary operator of drift; the human steers through specs and reviews in PRs.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/02-getting-started.md, the reader can: - install drift on macOS, Linux, or Windows - give drift to their LLM agent via drift skill - observe the agent writing specs, placing markers, and running drift todo - interpret a clean drift todo result
Prerequisites: - spec concept - marker concept - edge concept - chapter 1
Content requirements: - provide install instructions for macOS/Linux (curl pipe bash) and Windows (irm pipe iex) - show drift init creating .drift/ and a starter main.drift.xml - show the agent running drift skill to learn the workflow - show the agent writing a spec, placing a marker, and linking them (wrapped in ignore-span directives so the scanner does not treat examples as real markers) - show drift todo producing a clean result - explain that the human prompts the agent; the agent writes both specs and code - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docstart_ex) where the reader installs drift, gives it to their agent, and observes a clean drift todo

Overview: The reader learns how to introduce drift to an existing codebase. The agent surveys existing code, writes retroactive specs for current behavior, places markers around implementing code, links them, and resolves the resulting closures. This is the adoption workflow every new user goes through.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/03-how-to-add-drift-to-a-project.md, the reader can: - bootstrap drift on an existing codebase using their agent - describe the agent's role in surveying code and writing retroactive specs - place markers around existing implementing code - link markers to specs and resolve the initial closures - explain what belongs in .drift/ and what to commit to git
Prerequisites: - spec concept - marker concept - edge concept - baseline concept - scan concept - chapter 2
Content requirements: - walk through the agent surveying existing code to identify rules and behaviors worth specing - show the agent writing specs that capture existing behavior - show the agent placing markers around existing implementing code - show the agent linking markers to specs - show drift todo reporting closures from the new specs and markers - show the agent resolving closures to establish the baseline - explain what to commit to git (state.xml, baselines.bin) and what to gitignore (user-settings.xml, state.lock, friction.json) - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docaddp_ex) where the reader bootstraps drift on a small existing project with their agent

Overview: The reader learns how the agent adds a new feature: writes a spec capturing the intent, writes the implementing code, places a marker, links marker to spec, and verifies a clean state.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/04-how-to-add-a-feature.md, the reader can: - describe the agent workflow for adding a feature - identify what makes a good spec (compressed intent, specific enough to verify) - explain how markers connect specs to code - verify that a new feature is drift-clean
Prerequisites: - spec concept - marker concept - edge concept - chapter 3
Content requirements: - show the agent writing a spec from a natural-language prompt - show the agent writing implementing code and placing a marker - show the agent linking marker to spec - show drift todo clean after the feature is added - explain what makes a good spec vs a bad spec (too vague, too brittle) - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docfeat_ex) where the reader prompts the agent to add a small feature and verifies clean state

Overview: The reader learns how drift detects misalignment when the agent edits code inside a marker, how closures work, and how the agent uses the self-correction loop to catch its own mistakes.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/05-how-to-fix-a-bug.md, the reader can: - describe how closures detect misalignment between specs and code - interpret drift todo output when a marker drifts - trace drift through the citation graph - explain the self-correction loop: detect, review, decide, fix
Prerequisites: - closure concept - drift event concept - baseline concept - scan concept - chapter 4
Content requirements: - show the agent editing code inside a marker (NODE_CHANGED) - show the closure containing the changed marker, its linked spec, and any specs that cite that spec - show the agent reading drift diff to see what changed - show the agent deciding: spec wrong, code wrong, or intentional - show the agent fixing whichever side is wrong and resolving - explain the six drift event types and when each fires - explain that this self-correction loop is the core amplification: the agent catches its own mistakes before the human sees them - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docfix_ex) where the reader edits code inside a marker, observes the closure, and resolves it

Overview: The reader learns how drift behaves during refactoring. Moving code across marker boundaries changes the hash; drift cannot distinguish a pure refactor from a behavior change. The agent verifies semantics are preserved and resolves.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/06-how-to-refactor-a-module.md, the reader can: - explain why drift flags refactors (hash change is intentional) - describe the agent workflow for refactoring marked code - verify that a refactor preserved semantics
Prerequisites: - marker concept - chapter 4 - chapter 5
Content requirements: - show the agent moving code across a marker boundary - show drift flagging the change (NODE_CHANGED on the marker) - explain that drift does NOT distinguish refactor from behavior change — both produce hash changes, both need review - explain why this is intentional: refactors that accidentally change behavior are the most dangerous bugs - show the agent verifying semantics via drift diff, then resolving - explain marker placement strategy: keep markers on public entry points, not helpers - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docrefac_ex) where the reader refactors a function inside a marker and verifies semantics

Overview: The reader learns how to steer the project through spec edits. When a spec changes, drift propagates through the citation graph along the citer chain. Every spec that transitively cites the changed spec lands in the closure. The agent reads the closure as a work order and updates all affected code.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/07-how-to-change-a-spec.md, the reader can: - edit a spec to change project direction - trace drift propagation through the citation graph - describe how the citer chain works - update affected code based on closure membership
Prerequisites: - citer chain concept - closure concept - chapter 4 - chapter 5
Content requirements: - show editing a spec (changing a rule) - show drift propagating: every spec citing the changed spec via ref appears in the closure, transitively - show every marker linked to those specs also in the closure - show the agent reading the closure as a work order: here is all the code affected by this spec change - show the agent updating affected code to match the new spec - explain the citer chain: cited changes, citers are suspect, transitive to fixpoint - explain that this is the control plane in action: one spec edit shows all downstream impact - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docsteer_ex) where the reader edits a spec, observes propagation, and has the agent update affected code

Overview: The reader learns how to cleanly remove a feature from a drift-tracked project: delete the spec, remove the marker, unlink, and resolve the NODE_REMOVED closure.
Learning objectives: after reading docs/08-how-to-remove-a-feature.md, the reader can: - remove a spec and its marker cleanly - resolve NODE_REMOVED closures - verify no orphan state remains after removal
Prerequisites: - edge concept - chapter 4
Content requirements: - show the agent deleting a spec from the *.drift.xml file - show the agent removing the marker lines from the code file - show drift todo reporting NODE_REMOVED for both spec and marker - show the agent unlinking the marker from the spec - show the agent resolving the closures - show drift todo clean after removal - explain that leaving orphan markers or specs without cleanup produces persistent drift - include a hands-on exercise (marker: docrem_ex) where the reader removes a feature and verifies clean state
